lessons.title: Common Backtesting Mistakes That Hide Costs: Unrealistic Fills and Look-Ahead Bias

children.text: Everything so far assumed the gross return going into your cost model was honest. It often is not. Two methodology mistakes, look-ahead bias and unrealistic fills, inflate gross returns before a single rupee of transaction cost or slippage is even applied, and a perfect Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 cost model bolted onto an already-inflated gross number still produces a backtest that lies, just for a new reason.
Look-Ahead Bias: Trading on Information From the Future

markDefs.definition: Using data in a backtest that would not actually have been available at the simulated moment of the trading decision, giving the strategy an unfair, impossible view of the future.

children.text: happens whenever a backtest uses data that would not actually have existed yet at the moment it simulates a decision being made. It rarely looks like a mistake in the code, it usually looks like perfectly ordinary data handling.

cells: Under SEBI's listing regulations, quarterly results must be disclosed within 45 days of quarter-end, not on the quarter-end date itself. Trading on a March 31 number as of March 31 uses data that would not exist for another month and a half.
A backtest using a company's most recently restated numbers is using information that was only available after a later correction, not what investors saw when the original results were released.
Using the Nifty 500's current constituent list to backtest a strategy over the last five years silently excludes stocks that fell out of the index (and often fell in price) before they were removed.
Corporate action adjustments applied before the ex-date
Adjusting historical prices for a stock split or bonus issue before the actual ex-date lets a strategy react to an event before it had happened.

children.text: Unrealistic Fills: Trading at a Price You Could Not Have Gotten

The single most common unrealistic fill is subtle enough to survive in production code for years: a signal computed from a day's closing price, filled at that same day's closing price. In reality, you cannot know a day's official close until the market has finished trading for the day, at which point the opportunity to transact at that price has already passed. A signal generated from Day T's close can only realistically be filled at Day T+1's open, or later.
Worked Example: The Cost of a Missing One-Day Shift

A weekly breakout strategy, 52 entries a year, generates its signal from Friday's close and, in a naive backtest, fills at that same Friday close. Correctly filled at Monday's open instead, this stock's price has typically already gapped in the direction the breakout signal detected, since other market participants react to the same public information over the weekend. Across this strategy's trade history, that gap averages 0.12% against the strategy on every entry.

body.text: 6.24 percentage points of CAGR vanished here purely from a fill-timing assumption, before Chapter 2's transaction costs or Chapter 3's spread and market impact are even applied. A backtest with this bug and a perfect cost model would still report a badly inflated net return, because the gross number feeding into that cost model was already wrong.

children.text: Combined Effect: How This Compounds With the Cost Stack

Look-ahead bias and unrealistic fills are a different category of error from everything in Chapters 1 through 4. Transaction costs, spread, and market impact take a correct gross return and reduce it to a correct net return. Look-ahead bias and unrealistic fills corrupt the gross return itself, before it ever reaches the cost model. Fix the cost model without fixing this, and you have simply built a more precise cost calculation on top of a number that was never real to begin with.
The Fix: Shift Signals Before You Fill Them

body.caption: The missing .shift(1) is one of the most common look-ahead bugs in pandas-based backtests
body.code:
# WRONG: signal and fill use the same day's close
df["signal"] = df["close"] > df["close"].rolling(60).max().shift(1)
df["fill_price"] = df["close"]  # same day as the signal, impossible in practice

# CORRECT: signal is known at Day T's close, fill happens at Day T+1's open
df["signal"] = df["close"] > df["close"].rolling(60).max().shift(1)
df["fill_price"] = df["open"].shift(-1)  # tomorrow's open, relative to the signal day

# A quick sanity check worth running on every backtest:
# the fill_price column should never be knowable at the moment
# the signal column is computed. If it is, something is shifted wrong.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A backtest computes a signal from Thursday's closing price and fills the trade at that same Thursday's closing price. What is the most accurate description of the problem?
options: There is no problem, closing price is a standard reference point for backtests
This is an unrealistic fill: the official close is not knowable until after trading ends, so a trade cannot realistically execute at the same price the signal was computed from
The problem is transaction costs were not applied, not the fill timing
The problem only matters for strategies that trade options, not cash equity
body.explanation: The close is only final once the trading session has ended, by which point it is no longer a price you can transact at. This is a fill-timing problem, not a cost problem, and no amount of adding transaction costs or slippage afterward fixes it. The correct fix is filling at the next available price after the signal, typically the following session's open.

body.text: A cost model, however precise, cannot rescue a backtest whose gross return was never real. Look-ahead bias and unrealistic fills corrupt the number the cost model starts from, and in this lesson's example that corruption alone was worth more CAGR points than most of the individual cost components covered in Chapters 2 and 3.

points: Look-ahead bias uses data that would not actually have existed at the simulated decision point, common sources include fundamentals dated at quarter-end rather than announcement date, restated financials, and today's index membership applied to past periods.

The most common unrealistic fill is computing a signal from a day's closing price and filling the trade at that same closing price, which is not achievable in practice since the close is only final after trading ends.
In this lesson's worked example, correcting fill timing alone reduced gross CAGR from 20.00% to 13.76%, a 6.24-point correction that happens before any transaction cost or slippage model is applied.
A missing .shift(1) between signal computation and fill price assignment is one of the most common and hardest-to-notice sources of this bug in real backtesting code.
